draft.title: The Freedom Ride
card: In 1965 a group of Sydney University students travelled by bus through country towns in New South Wales. Charles Perkins, an Aboriginal student, led the group, called Student Action for Aborigines (SAFA).
They went to expose racial segregation, which meant Aboriginal people were kept apart from white people or turned away. It happened at places such as swimming pools, cinemas and shops.
At Walgett the students protested at the RSL club, which refused to admit Aboriginal ex-servicemen. At Moree they challenged the council pool, which barred Aboriginal children.
Newspapers and television reported the protests across Australia. Many people learnt about discrimination in their own country, and this added public pressure for change.
draft.remember: The Freedom Ride used protest and media attention to expose everyday racial discrimination.

a.q: What was the main aim of the 1965 Freedom Ride?
opts: To expose racial segregation in country towns
To win Aboriginal people the right to vote
To end the removal of children from families
To protest against the 150th anniversary celebrations
a.why: The students travelled to country towns to show how Aboriginal people were kept apart in pools, cinemas and shops. The protest on 26 January 1938 was a different event and was held in Sydney, not on a bus tour.
a.clue: Think about what the students wanted people to see in the towns.

b.q: Students in a bus are refused entry to a town pool because Aboriginal children travelling with them are barred. They protest and a reporter films it. How does this match the Freedom Ride?
opts: Protest and media coverage exposed discrimination
Their protest changed the law in the whole state
It was a march by the students to Parliament House
The students ran the pool to show how it could work
b.why: The Freedom Ride used protest at local places, and media coverage spread the news to the public. It did not directly change the law, so the option about changing the law across the state goes beyond what the card says.
b.clue: Remember what happened after the newspapers and television arrived.

a.best: To expose racial segregation in country towns

b.best: Protest and media coverage exposed discrimination

problems.detail: The scenario says the students 'protest' and 'a reporter films it', and only the right option mentions protest and media. A student can match words to pick it without knowing the idea. The other options (a march to Parliament House, running the pool) are also implausible, so the question is very easy.

proposal.title: The Freedom Ride
card: In 1965 a group of Sydney University students travelled by bus through country towns in New South Wales. Charles Perkins, an Aboriginal student, led the group, called Student Action for Aborigines (SAFA).
They went to expose racial segregation, which meant Aboriginal people were kept apart from white people or turned away. It happened at places such as swimming pools, cinemas and shops.
At Walgett the students protested at the RSL club, which refused to admit Aboriginal ex-servicemen. At Moree they challenged the council pool, which barred Aboriginal children.

Newspapers and television reported the protests across Australia. Segregation did not end at once, but many people learnt about discrimination in their own country, and this added public pressure for change.
proposal.remember: The Freedom Ride used protest and media attention to expose everyday racial discrimination.

a.q: What was the main aim of the 1965 Freedom Ride?
opts: To expose racial segregation in country towns
To win Aboriginal people the right to vote
To end the removal of children from families
To protest against the 150th anniversary celebrations
a.why: The students travelled to country towns to show how Aboriginal people were kept apart in pools, cinemas and shops. The protest about the 150th anniversary was a different event, held in Sydney in 1938, not a bus tour in 1965.
a.clue: Think about what the students wanted people to see in the towns.

b.q: A historian says the Freedom Ride mattered far beyond the towns the bus visited. Which reason best supports this view?
opts: News reports showed Australians the discrimination
It ended segregation in all NSW towns straight away
It was run by the government to change national laws
It focused on laws in Canberra, not on local places
b.why: Newspapers and television carried the protests across Australia, so people far from Walgett and Moree learnt about discrimination, which added pressure for change. It is tempting to think the ride ended segregation, but it did not end at once.
b.clue: Think about how people who never saw the towns found out.
